claim: Acute kidney injury has approximately 13 million cases per year globally.
source: The global burden of acute kidney injury is approximately 13 million cases a year (Ponce and Balbi, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ponce and Balbi, 2016.

claim: Acute kidney injury is associated with 1.7 million deaths per year worldwide.
source: It is associated with a high mortality (1.7 million deaths per year, worldwide) (Gameiro et al., 2018; Hoste et al., 2018; Mehta et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gameiro et al., 2018; Hoste et al., 2018; Mehta et al., 2016.

claim: Renal ischaemia followed by reperfusion is the most common cause of acute kidney injury.
source: Renal ischaemia followed by reperfusion, which can occur after cardiac surgery, renal transplant, or severe haemorrhage, is the most common cause of acute kidney injury (Lameire et al., 2006; Lameire and Vanholder, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lameire et al., 2006; Lameire and Vanholder, 2001.

claim: Sustained renal blood flow reductions occur after ischaemia and reperfusion in experimental studies and patients after kidney transplantation.
source: Sustained renal blood flow reductions occur after ischaemia and reperfusion, both in experimental studies and in patients after kidney transplantation (Cristol et al., 1996; Nijveldt et al., 2001; Ramaswamy et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cristol et al., 1996; Nijveldt et al., 2001; Ramaswamy et al., 2002.

claim: After short periods of ischaemia, blood flow to the renal cortex largely recovers following reperfusion, but medullary blood flow remains reduced for a prolonged period.
source: Following short periods of ischaemia, blood flow to the renal cortex largely recovers following reperfusion, but medullary blood flow remains reduced for a prolonged period, especially in the hypoxia-sensitive outer medulla
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and is consistent with the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Medullary no-reflow is a critical event for amplifying renal tissue injury following reperfusion.
source: Medullary no-reflow is a critical event for amplifying renal tissue injury following reperfusion (Conesa et al., 2001; Olof et al., 1991; Regner et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Conesa et al., 2001; Olof et al., 1991; Regner et al., 2009.

claim: In the brain and heart, contractile pericytes on capillaries play a key role in reducing blood flow after ischaemia.
source: Indeed, in the brain and heart contractile pericytes on capillaries play a key role in reducing blood flow after ischaemia (Hall et al., 2014; O'Farrell et al., 2017; Yemisci et al., 2009) because capillaries remain constricted by pericytes even when blood flow is restored to upstream arterioles.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hall et al., 2014; O'Farrell et al., 2017; Yemisci et al., 2009.

claim: In the retina, capillary constriction is mediated by α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA) based actomyosin-mediated contraction of capillary pericytes.
source: In the retina it has been shown that this capillary constriction is mediated by α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA) based actomyosin-mediated contraction of capillary pericytes (Alarcon-Martinez et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Alarcon-Martinez et al., 2019.

claim: Pericyte populations in the kidney, particularly those in the descending vasa recta, are associated with α-SMA expression and contractility.
source: As in the retina, pericyte populations in the kidney, particularly those in the descending vasa recta, are associated with α-SMA expression and contractility (Park et al., 1997; Shaw et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Park et al., 1997; Shaw et al., 2018.

claim: Pericytes play a key role in regulating renal medullary blood flow.
source: They play a key role in regulating renal medullary blood flow (Crawford et al., 2012; Pallone and Silldorff, 2001)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Crawford et al., 2012; Pallone and Silldorff, 2001.

claim: Rho kinase is an important regulator of pericyte contractility.
source: An important regulator of pericyte contractility is the Rho kinase pathway (Durham et al., 2014; Kutcher et al., 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Durham et al., 2014; Kutcher et al., 2007.

claim: Rho kinase inhibits myosin phosphatase, thus increasing phosphorylation of myosin light chain (MLC) and increasing contraction.
source: which inhibits myosin phosphatase, thus increasing phosphorylation of myosin light chain (MLC) and increasing contraction (Kimura et al., 1996; Maeda et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kimura et al., 1996; Maeda et al., 2003.

claim: Overactivity of Rho kinase may play a key role in hypertension, diabetes, and kidney ischaemia.
source: Overactivity of Rho kinase may play a key role in hypertension and diabetes, as well as in kidney ischaemia (Jahani et al., 2018; Kushiyama et al., 2013; Peng et al., 2008; Soga et al., 2011; Versteilen et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jahani et al., 2018; Kushiyama et al., 2013; Peng et al., 2008; Soga et al., 2011; Versteilen et al., 2006.

claim: Rho kinase may regulate pericyte contractility by modulating actin polymerisation.
source: Rho kinase may also regulate pericyte contractility by modulating actin polymerisation (Kureli et al., 2020; Kutcher and Herman, 2009; Maekawa et al., 1999; Zhang et al., 2018a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kureli et al., 2020; Kutcher and Herman, 2009; Maekawa et al., 1999; Zhang et al., 2018a.

claim: In ischaemia, Rho kinase inhibits myosin phosphatase via inactivation of endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS).
source: In ischaemia, an important pathway by which Rho kinase inhibits myosin phosphatase is via inactivation of endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) (Versteilen et al., 2006)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Versteilen et al., 2006.

claim: Rho kinase is an important effector of vasoconstrictors such as endothelin-1 and angiotensin II.
source: Rho kinase is an important effector of vasoconstrictors such as endothelin-1 (Prakash et al., 2008; Wilhelm et al., 1999; Yamamoto et al., 2000) and angiotensin II (Rupérez et al., 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Prakash et al., 2008; Wilhelm et al., 1999; Yamamoto et al., 2000 for endothelin-1, and Rupérez et al., 2005 for angiotensin II.

claim: Peritubular pericytes are damaged in cortical tissue of cadaveric renal allografts following ischaemia-reperfusion.
source: However, peritubular pericytes are damaged in cortical tissue of cadaveric renal allografts following ischaemia-reperfusion (Kwon et al., 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kwon et al., 2008.

claim: Ischaemia for 1 hr decreased perfusion of the renal medulla by ~90%.
source: Ischaemia for 1 hr decreased perfusion of the renal medulla and cortex by ~90% (both P < 0.0001 vs. control; assessed with laser Doppler: Figure 1a and b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data measured with laser Doppler and shown in Figure 1a.

claim: After 30 min reperfusion, blood flow recovered to 49% of control in the medulla.
source: After 30 min reperfusion, blood flow recovered to 49% of control (significantly reduced, P = 0.005, Figure 1a) in the medulla
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: After 30 min reperfusion, blood flow recovered to 75% in the cortex.
source: but to 75% in the cortex (P = 0.047, Figure 1b; Regner et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b and a citation to Regner et al., 2009.

claim: After 60 min reperfusion, medullary perfusion remained compromised at 40% of the control level.
source: After 60 min reperfusion, medullary perfusion remained compromised at 40% of the control level (P = 0.017, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: After 60 min reperfusion, cortical perfusion had fully recovered.
source: but cortical perfusion had fully recovered (to ~20% above the control value, not significant, P = 0.092, Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Medullary perfusion was reduced after 30 min of post-ischaemic reperfusion by ~50% compared with control kidneys.
source: Medullary perfusion (assessed in slices of fixed kidney as the total intensity of FITC-albumin summed over the ROIs) was reduced after 30 min of post-ischaemic reperfusion (51 stacks, 6 animals) by ~50% compared with control kidneys (52 stacks, 7 animals).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1f, assessed using FITC-albumin intensity in fixed kidney slices.

claim: Treatment with hydroxyfasudil increased medullary perfusion 2.3-fold at 30 min reperfusion compared with non-treated ischaemic kidneys.
source: Treatment with HF increased medullary perfusion 2.3-fold at this time compared with non-treated ischaemic kidneys (20 stacks, 4 animals).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: Cortex perfusion after 30 min of reperfusion after ischaemia was reduced by ~23.5% compared with control kidneys.
source: Cortex perfusion (assessed as in c-e) after 30 min of reperfusion after ischaemia was reduced by ~23.5% compared with control kidneys.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: Treatment with hydroxyfasudil increased cortex perfusion by 25% at 30 min reperfusion compared with non-treated ischaemic kidneys.
source: Treatment with HF (I/R + HF) increased cortex perfusion by 25% at this time compared with non-treated ischaemic kidneys (I/R).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: The total perfused capillary length in the medulla was reduced by 35% after ischaemia and reperfusion.
source: The total perfused capillary length in 100 µm deep confocal z-stacks (frame size 640.17 × 640.17 µm) was reduced by 35% (contralateral control 14689 ± 3477 µm vs. ischaemia 9527 ±1183 µm, P = 0.038)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from confocal imaging shown in Figure 2e.

claim: The number of perfused capillary segments in the medulla was reduced by 54% after ischaemia and reperfusion.
source: the number of perfused capillary segments was reduced by 54% (control 530 ± 82 vs. ischaemia 244 ± 30, P = 0.03)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from confocal imaging shown in Figure 2f.

claim: The overall perfused microvascular volume fraction in the medulla was reduced by 51% after ischaemia and reperfusion.
source: and the overall perfused microvascular volume fraction was reduced by 51% (control 0.116 ± 0.006 vs. ischaemia 0.057 ± 0.006, P = 0.003; Figure 2e–g).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from confocal imaging shown in Figure 2g.

claim: A small percentage of afferent and efferent arterioles, and glomeruli, were not perfused in control conditions.
source: Furthermore, although a small percentage of afferent and efferent arterioles, and glomeruli, were not perfused in control conditions, this percentage did not increase significantly after ischaemia (Figure 3a, b and g)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3g.

claim: The arterioles' diameter was not reduced after ischaemia compared with those in non-ischaemic kidneys.
source: and the arterioles' diameter was not reduced compared with those in non-ischaemic kidneys (Figure 3a, b, h and i).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3h and i.

claim: Upstream arteries are not constricted after ischaemia.
source: Similarly, it has been reported that upstream arteries are not constricted after ischaemia (Yamamoto et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yamamoto et al., 2002.

claim: The total perfused peritubular capillary length in the cortex was reduced by 67% after ischaemia and reperfusion.
source: In contrast, the total perfused peritubular capillary length in the 100 µm deep z-stacks (control 16441 ± 1577 µm vs. ischaemia 5411 ±2735 µm, reduced by 67%, P = 0.03)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The number of perfused peritubular capillary segments in the cortex was reduced by 36.5% after ischaemia and reperfusion.
source: the number of perfused capillary segments (control 550 ± 32 µm vs. ischaemia 349 ±54, reduced by 36.5%, P = 0.01)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: The overall perfused peritubular capillary volume fraction in the cortex was reduced by 50% after ischaemia and reperfusion.
source: and the overall perfused peritubular capillary volume fraction (control 0.12 ± 0.01 vs. ischaemia 0.06 ± 0.02, reduced by 50%, P = 0.01) were greatly reduced in the cortex when compared with non-ischaemic kidneys (Figure 3d–f).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3f.

claim: The effect of ischaemia and reperfusion is predominantly on the microvasculature, that is the peritubular cortical capillaries and the vasa recta, rather than on arteriolar segments of the kidney circulation.
source: Thus, the effect of ischaemia and reperfusion is predominantly on the microvasculature, that is the peritubular cortical capillaries and the vasa recta, rather than on arteriolar segments of the kidney circulation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that arterioles are not affected while capillaries are significantly constricted.

claim: In control kidneys, only 9.7% of the descending vasa recta (DVR) capillaries were blocked.
source: Higher magnification images demonstrated that, in control kidneys, only 9.7% of the descending vasa recta (DVR) capillaries were blocked (Figures 2b and 4d)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: After ischaemia and 30 mins reperfusion, 78% of the DVR capillaries were blocked.
source: However, after ischaemia and 30 mins reperfusion, 78% of the DVR capillaries were blocked (Figures 2c and 4a–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: At block sites, the diameter of the FITC-albumin lumenal labelling was significantly lower in ischaemic DVR capillaries compared with that at block sites in non-ischaemic controls.
source: At block sites, the diameter of the FITC-albumin lumenal labelling at the final position blood reached was significantly lower in ischaemic DVR capillaries compared with that at the much smaller number of block sites in non-ischaemic controls (control 6.5 ± 0.3 µm vs. ischaemia 3.5 ± 0.4 µm; P = 0.039, Figure 4e).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: An ischaemia-induced constriction of the DVR promotes blockage, which persists even after reperfusion.
source: Thus, an ischaemia-induced constriction of the DVR promotes blockage, which persists even after reperfusion.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing reduced diameter at block sites after ischaemia.

claim: Red blood cells were associated with only a small percentage of blockage sites in ischaemic kidneys (5.8% of 85 blockages).
source: Red blood cells (RBCs, indicated by yellow arrowheads, labelled for glycophorin A) were associated with a small percentage of blockage sites (indicated by blue arrowheads) in ischaemic rat kidneys (5.8% of 85 blockages from 137 vessels analysed from two animals)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a, b.

claim: The mean blockage-pericyte distance was 4.87 ± 0.33 µm after ischaemia and reperfusion.
source: The mean blockage-pericyte distance was 4.87 ± 0.33 µm after ischaemia and reperfusion, which is less than a quarter of the distance between DVR pericytes (22.85 ± 0.93 µm, from 118 pericyte pairs).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: The distance between DVR pericytes is 22.85 ± 0.93 µm.
source: The mean blockage-pericyte distance was 4.87 ± 0.33 µm after ischaemia and reperfusion, which is less than a quarter of the distance between DVR pericytes (22.85 ± 0.93 µm, from 118 pericyte pairs).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from measurements of pericyte spacing.

claim: These data are consistent with pericyte constriction generating the DVR blockages.
source: Thus, these data are consistent with pericyte constriction generating the DVR blockages.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing blockages occur near pericyte somata.

claim: After ischaemia and reperfusion, the DVR diameter was significantly reduced (by 41%) near the pericyte somata compared with non-ischaemic kidneys.
source: After ischaemia and reperfusion, the diameter was significantly reduced (by 41%, P = 0.0001) near the pericyte somata compared with non-ischaemic kidneys, but less reduced further from the somata.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: The diameter significantly increased with distance from the somata after ischaemia and reperfusion.
source: The diameter significantly increased with distance from the somata after ischaemia and reperfusion (P = 0.039 comparing the slope of the best-fit ischaemia regression line with zero) but not in control conditions (P = 0.084)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: eGCX is fairly uniformly present along capillaries, and this was not altered after ischaemia.
source: Labelling showed that eGCX is fairly uniformly present along capillaries, and this was not altered after ischaemia (Figure 4—figure supplement 1f-g).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1f-g.

claim: There was no correlation between eGCX intensity and capillary diameter in control or ischaemic conditions.
source: There was no correlation between eGCX intensity and capillary diameter in control or ischaemic conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1h.

claim: eGCX is not particularly associated with pericytes.
source: Thus, eGCX is not particularly associated with pericytes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1f)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1f.

claim: The co-location of diameter reduction and blockages with pericyte somata presumably reflects pericyte process contraction rather than obstruction by eGCX.
source: so the co-location of diameter reduction and blockages with pericyte somata presumably reflects pericyte process contraction rather than obstruction by eGCX.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing eGCX is not associated with pericytes or blockages.

claim: Ischaemia and reperfusion reduced the mean capillary diameter in the cortex from 10.8 ± 0.2 to 8.1 ± 0.5 µm.
source: This reduced the mean capillary diameter (averaged over all positions measured) from 10.8 ± 0.2 to 8.1 ± 0.5 µm (P < 0.0001).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from two-photon microscopy in vivo.

claim: The distance of blockages to the nearest pericyte soma in the cortex was 4.12 ± 0.39 µm.
source: To quantify whether ischaemia-evoked blockages occurred disproportionately close to pericytes, we measured the distance of 15 blockages to the nearest pericyte soma. This distance was 4.12 ± 0.39 µm, which is only 10% of the mean distance between peritubular cortical pericytes (41.3 ± 2.6 µm, from 103 pericyte pairs).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from two-photon microscopy in vivo.

claim: The mean distance between peritubular cortical pericytes is 41.3 ± 2.6 µm.
source: This distance was 4.12 ± 0.39 µm, which is only 10% of the mean distance between peritubular cortical pericytes (41.3 ± 2.6 µm, from 103 pericyte pairs).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from two-photon microscopy in vivo.

claim: Ischaemia and reperfusion reduced the cortical capillary diameter by 40% at the pericyte somata.
source: A plot of capillary diameter versus distance from pericyte somata (Figure 5d) showed that ischaemia and reperfusion reduced the diameter by 40% at the somata (control 11.2 ± 0.5 vs. ischaemia 6.76 ± 1.05 µm, P = 0.001)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Ischaemia and reperfusion had no significant effect on cortical capillary diameter far from the pericyte somata.
source: with no significant effect on diameter far from the somata (control 10.3 ± 0.2 µm vs. ischaemia 9.6 ± 0.5 µm, P = 0.115).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The diameter increased significantly with distance from the pericyte somata after ischaemia in the cortex.
source: As in the medulla, the diameter increased significantly with distance from the pericyte somata after ischaemia (P = 0.046 comparing the slope of the best-fit regression line with zero) while in control conditions it did not (diameter decreased insignificantly with distance, P = 0.10).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Capillaries are constricted specifically near cortical pericytes.
source: Thus, capillaries are constricted specifically near cortical pericytes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing diameter reduction specifically at pericyte somata.

claim: The mean distance between pericytes in the medulla (23 μm) is roughly half that in the cortex (41 μm).
source: The mean distance between pericytes in the medulla (23 μm, see above) is roughly half that in the cortex (41 μm, see above).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental measurements of pericyte spacing reported earlier in the manuscript.

claim: DVR pericytes show many circumferential processes around the capillaries, while cortical pericytes exhibit mainly longitudinal processes running along the capillary with only a small number of circumferential processes.
source: Furthermore, in general the morphology of pericytes differs in these two regions, with DVR pericytes showing many circumferential processes around the capillaries, while cortical pericytes exhibit mainly longitudinal processes running along the capillary with only a small number of circumferential processes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Hydroxyfasudil applied at the time of reperfusion significantly inhibited the decrease of renal medullary perfusion seen after ischaemia-reperfusion.
source: The Rho kinase inhibitor, hydroxyfasudil (3 mg/kg; i.v.), applied at the time of reperfusion to mimic a possible therapeutic intervention, significantly inhibited the decrease of renal medullary perfusion seen after ischaemia-reperfusion (Figure 1a and e–f).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a and e–f.

claim: In vivo, blood flow in the medulla (after 30 min reperfusion) was increased 3.8-fold compared to ischaemia without hydroxyfasudil.
source: In vivo, blood flow in the medulla (after 30 min reperfusion) was increased 3.8-fold compared to ischaemia without hydroxyfasudil (P = 0.002, Figure 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Hydroxyfasudil induced a faster recovery of medullary blood flow than BQ123, an endothelin-A receptor antagonist.
source: Hydroxyfasudil induced a faster recovery of medullary blood flow than BQ123 (0.5 mg/kg, i.v.), an endothelin-A receptor antagonist (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Both hydroxyfasudil and BQ123 resulted in blood flow at 30 mins reperfusion that was not significantly different from the control value and was significantly higher than the flow seen after ischaemia without either drug.
source: but both resulted in blood flow at 30 mins reperfusion that was not significantly different from the control value (P = 0.8 and 0.38, respectively) and was significantly higher than the flow seen after ischaemia without either drug (P = 0.01 for both drugs).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Valsartan, an angiotensin II type 1 (AT1) receptor antagonist, speeded the initial post-ischaemic recovery of medullary blood flow, but did not return it to baseline by 30 min reperfusion.
source: In contrast, the angiotensin II type 1 (AT1) receptor antagonist valsartan (1 mg/kg i.v.) speeded the initial post-ischaemic recovery of medullary blood flow, but did not return it to baseline by 30 min reperfusion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c.

claim: In the cortex, blood flow recovery on reperfusion was speeded by hydroxyfasudil and, after 30 min of reperfusion, was increased 1.48-fold compared to ischaemia alone.
source: In the cortex, blood flow recovery on reperfusion was speeded by hydroxyfasudil and, after 30 min of reperfusion, was increased 1.48-fold compared to ischaemia alone (P = 0.02, Figure 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Activation of Rho kinase (in part downstream of ischaemia-evoked activation of endothelin-A receptors) contributes to ischaemia-evoked pericyte-mediated capillary constriction.
source: These data suggest that, in the medulla especially, activation of Rho kinase (in part downstream of ischaemia-evoked activation of endothelin-A receptors [Prakash et al., 2008; Wilhelm et al., 1999; Yamamoto et al., 2000]) contributes to ischaemia-evoked pericyte-mediated capillary constriction.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that Rho kinase inhibition and endothelin-A receptor antagonism improve blood flow, and is supported by citations.

claim: Treatment with hydroxyfasudil during post-ischaemic reperfusion prevented medullary no-reflow after ischaemia and reperfusion: the blood volume was increased 2.3-fold compared to ischaemia alone.
source: Treatment with hydroxyfasudil during post-ischaemic reperfusion prevented medullary no-reflow after ischaemia and reperfusion: the blood volume was increased 2.3-fold compared to ischaemia alone (P = 0.003, Figure 1e–f)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e–f.

claim: Hydroxyfasudil increased ~2.9-fold the total perfused medullary capillary length.
source: Hydroxyfasudil also increased ~2.9-fold the total perfused medullary capillary length (P = 0.043)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Hydroxyfasudil increased ~2.9 fold the number of perfused capillary segments in the medulla.
source: ~2.9 fold the number of perfused capillary segments (P = 0.02)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: Hydroxyfasudil increased ~2-fold the perfused volume fraction in medulla.
source: and ~2-fold the perfused volume fraction (P = 0.0031) in medulla (Figure 2d–g).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2g.

claim: In the renal cortex, hydroxyfasudil given on reperfusion increased perfusion (blood volume) ~1.25-fold.
source: In the renal cortex, hydroxyfasudil given on reperfusion increased perfusion (blood volume)~1.25-fold (P = 0.0098; Figure 1e and g)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e and g.

claim: Hydroxyfasudil increased the total perfused length of capillaries, the number of perfused capillary segments and the blood volume fraction in the cortex to values that were not significantly different from those in non-ischaemic kidneys.
source: and increased the total perfused length of capillaries, the number of perfused capillary segments and the blood volume fraction to values that were not significantly different from those in non-ischaemic kidneys (Figure 3c–f).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c–f.

claim: Hydroxyfasudil had no effect on the diameter of afferent or efferent arterioles feeding and leaving the glomeruli.
source: However, it had no effect on the diameter of afferent or efferent arterioles feeding and leaving the glomeruli (Figure 3h and i).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3h and i.

claim: Hydroxyfasudil reduced the constriction evoked at DVR pericyte somata by ischaemia and reperfusion, increasing the diameter from 4.5 ± 0.5 µm without hydroxyfasudil to 8.0 ± 0.4 µm with the drug.
source: In contrast, hydroxyfasudil reduced the constriction evoked at DVR pericyte somata by ischaemia and reperfusion, increasing the diameter from 4.5 ± 0.5 µm without hydroxyfasudil to 8.0 ± 0.4 µm with the drug (P < 0.0001) (Figure 4g)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: Hydroxyfasudil reduced the percentage of DVR capillaries blocked from 78 ± 9% to 8 ± 5%.
source: and reduced the percentage of DVR capillaries blocked from 78 ± 9% to 8 ± 5% (P = 0.023), both of which are not significantly different from the values in non-ischaemic kidneys (Figure 4d and f).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Ischaemia induces, and hydroxyfasudil decreases, medullary no-reflow by specifically acting on DVR capillary pericytes rather than on upstream arterioles.
source: Thus, ischaemia induces, and hydroxyfasudil decreases, medullary no-reflow by specifically acting on DVR capillary pericytes rather than on upstream arterioles.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing hydroxyfasudil affects pericyte-mediated capillary constriction but not arteriole diameter.

claim: After ischaemia and reperfusion, phosphorylated MLC was increased ~11-fold for medullary pericytes.
source: After ischaemia and reperfusion, this was increased ~11-fold for medullary and five-fold for cortical pericytes (P = 0.0001 in both locations, Figure 6a–j).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6j.

claim: After ischaemia and reperfusion, phosphorylated MLC was increased five-fold for cortical pericytes.
source: After ischaemia and reperfusion, this was increased ~11-fold for medullary and five-fold for cortical pericytes (P = 0.0001 in both locations, Figure 6a–j).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6e.

claim: Hydroxyfasudil treatment after reperfusion reduced the increase in phosphorylated MLC so that the labelling was not significantly different from that in control kidneys.
source: Hydroxyfasudil treatment after reperfusion reduced this increase so that the labelling was not significantly different from that in control kidneys (P = 0.95 and P = 0.56, respectively; Figure 6a–j).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6e and j.

claim: 56% of DVR pericytes near blockage sites labelled for the contractile protein α-SMA.
source: Consistent with pericytes employing smooth muscle actomyosin, 56% of DVR pericytes near blockage sites labelled for the contractile protein α-SMA (Figure 6k–n; see also Park et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6k–n and a citation to Park et al., 1997.

claim: Kim-1 levels in the proximal tubules were elevated 81-fold by ischaemia and reperfusion.
source: Kim-1 levels in the proximal tubules were elevated 81-fold by ischaemia and reperfusion (P = 0.0004, Figure 7a, b and d)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7d.

claim: Treatment with hydroxyfasudil during reperfusion halved the Kim-1 labelling.
source: and treatment with hydroxyfasudil during reperfusion halved the Kim-1 labelling (P = 0.03, Figure 7c and d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7d.

claim: The long-lasting decrease of renal blood flow that follows transient ischaemia is generated by pericyte-mediated constriction and block of the descending vasa recta and cortical peritubular capillaries.
source: This paper demonstrates, for the first time, that the long-lasting decrease of renal blood flow that follows transient ischaemia is generated by pericyte-mediated constriction and block of the descending vasa recta and cortical peritubular capillaries, as schematised in the summary of Figure 8
evidence: The claim is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the experimental data presented.

claim: Post-ischaemic no-reflow can be reduced pharmacologically.
source: and that this post-ischaemic no-reflow can be reduced pharmacologically.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data showing hydroxyfasudil reduces no-reflow.

claim: Sites of ischaemia-evoked medullary and cortical capillary block were associated with pericyte locations.
source: We found in vivo that sites of ischaemia-evoked medullary and cortical capillary block were associated with pericyte locations.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing blockages occur near pericyte somata.

claim: After ischaemia and reperfusion, the diameters of descending vasa recta and peritubular capillaries were reduced specifically near pericyte somata.
source: Furthermore, after ischaemia and reperfusion, the diameters of descending vasa recta and peritubular capillaries were reduced specifically near pericyte somata, which extend contractile circumferential processes around the capillaries.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing diameter reduction at pericyte somata.

claim: Cortical arteriole diameters were not reduced after ischaemia and reperfusion.
source: In contrast, cortical arteriole diameters were not reduced and glomeruli remained perfused.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3h and i.

claim: Glomeruli remained perfused after ischaemia and reperfusion.
source: In contrast, cortical arteriole diameters were not reduced and glomeruli remained perfused.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3g.

claim: The fact that capillary diameters are reduced specifically near pericyte somata establishes that this is due to a contraction of the circumferential processes of pericytes.
source: The fact that capillary diameters are reduced specifically near pericyte somata establishes that this is due to a contraction of the circumferential processes of pericytes, and not (for example) due to a decrease in overall perfusion pressure (which would also reduce the diameter of capillaries away from pericyte somata).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing diameter reduction is localized to pericyte somata.

claim: Pericyte-mediated capillary constriction is a major therapeutic target for treating post-ischaemic renal no-reflow.
source: Together, these data establish pericyte-mediated capillary constriction as a major therapeutic target for treating post-ischaemic renal no-reflow.
evidence: The claim is the main conclusion of the study, inferred from all the experimental data.

claim: Pericyte-mediated constriction of renal capillaries may reflect reduced Ca2+ pumping in ischaemia, raising [Ca2+]i which activates contraction.
source: Pericyte-mediated constriction of renal capillaries may reflect reduced Ca2+ pumping in ischaemia, raising [Ca2+]i which activates contraction, as for CNS pericytes (Hall et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on analogy to CNS pericytes and supported by a citation to Hall et al., 2014.

claim: Constriction may partly reflect a release of angiotensin II and endothelin-1 which raise [Ca2+]i and Rho kinase activity.
source: Constriction may also partly reflect a release of angiotensin II (Allred et al., 2000; Boer et al., 1997; da Silveira et al., 2010; Miyata et al., 1999; Sanchez-Pozos et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2004) and endothelin-1 (Afyouni et al., 2015; Jones et al., 2020; Sanchez-Pozos et al., 2012) which raise [Ca2+]i and Rho kinase activity (Lee et al., 2014; Shimokawa and Rashid, 2007)
evidence: The claim is speculative, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Blocking endothelin-A receptors improved post-ischaemic renal blood flow.
source: since we found that blocking endothelin-A receptors and, to a lesser extent, angiotensin II receptors improved post-ischaemic renal blood flow.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Blocking angiotensin II receptors improved post-ischaemic renal blood flow to a lesser extent than blocking endothelin-A receptors.
source: since we found that blocking endothelin-A receptors and, to a lesser extent, angiotensin II receptors improved post-ischaemic renal blood flow.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Vasoconstricting endothelin-A and angiotensin II type 1 (AT1) receptors are located on pericytes along the descending vasa recta and regulate contractility at pericyte sites.
source: Consistent with this, it has been demonstrated that vasoconstricting endothelin-A (Crawford et al., 2012; Wendel et al., 2006) and angiotensin II type 1 (AT1) (Crawford et al., 2012; Miyata et al., 1999; Terada et al., 1993) receptors are located on pericytes along the descending vasa recta and regulate contractility at pericyte sites (Crawford et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Crawford et al., 2012; Wendel et al., 2006; Miyata et al., 1999; Terada et al., 1993.

claim: Endothelin-1 and angiotensin II evoke potent vasoconstriction of the descending vasa recta mainly through endothelin-A and angiotensin II type 1 (AT1) receptors.
source: Additionally, endothelin-1 and angiotensin II evoke potent vasoconstriction of the descending vasa recta mainly through endothelin-A (Silldorff et al., 1995) and angiotensin II type 1 (AT1) (Rhinehart et al., 2003) receptors.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Silldorff et al., 1995 and Rhinehart et al., 2003.

claim: Some pericyte populations in the kidney, especially those in the descending vasa recta, express α-SMA and regulate capillary blood flow.
source: It has long been known that some pericyte populations in the kidney, especially those in the descending vasa recta, express α-SMA and regulate capillary blood flow (Park et al., 1997; Shaw et al., 2018), presumably via actomyosin-based contractility.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Park et al., 1997; Shaw et al., 2018.

claim: A potentially important physiological role for the presence of α-SMA in the descending vasa recta pericytes is the ability of these pericytes to regulate blood flow distribution within the renal medulla.
source: A potentially important physiological role for the presence of α-SMA in the descending vasa recta pericytes is the ability of these pericytes to regulate blood flow distribution within the renal medulla (Pallone and Silldorff, 2001; Park et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is speculative, supported by citations to Pallone and Silldorff, 2001; Park et al., 1997.

claim: α-SMA protein was strongly labelled within the pericytes surrounding the descending vasa recta.
source: In agreement with other studies, we observed that α-SMA protein was strongly labelled within the pericytes surrounding the descending vasa recta (Figure 6k–n; see also Park et al., 1997), including in pericytes near ischaemia-evoked blockage sites.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6k–n and a citation to Park et al., 1997.

claim: Ischaemia increased MLC phosphorylation in pericytes and led to pericyte-mediated capillary constriction, consistent with actomyosin mediating the contractility of these cells.
source: Furthermore, ischaemia increased MLC phosphorylation in pericytes (Figure 6a–j) and led to pericyte-mediated capillary constriction, consistent with actomyosin mediating the contractility of these cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing increased MLC phosphorylation and capillary constriction.

claim: Rho kinase inhibits the MLC dephosphorylation required to relax pericytes, mainly by inhibiting eNOS activity, thus promoting constriction.
source: Rho kinase, a key downstream effector of both endothelin-1 and angiotensin II, inhibits the MLC dephosphorylation required to relax pericytes (Kimura et al., 1996; Maeda et al., 2003), mainly by inhibiting eNOS activity (Versteilen et al., 2006),thus promoting constriction (Hartmann et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kimura et al., 1996; Maeda et al., 2003; Versteilen et al., 2006; Hartmann et al., 2021.

claim: Blocking Rho kinase with hydroxyfasudil reduced MLC phosphorylation in pericytes after ischaemia.
source: We found that blocking Rho kinase with hydroxyfasudil reduced MLC phosphorylation in pericytes after ischaemia (Figure 6a–j)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6a–j.

claim: Blocking Rho kinase reversed ischaemia-evoked pericyte-mediated capillary constriction.
source: and reversed ischaemia-evoked pericyte-mediated capillary constriction (hydroxyfasudil increased the capillary diameter specifically at pericyte somata (Figure 4g) in ischaemic animals, implying that the effects of Rho kinase inhibition were on renal pericytes rather than an extra-renal systemic action).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: Rho kinase block reduces acute kidney injury.
source: This could explain why Rho kinase block reduces acute kidney injury (Kentrup et al., 2011; Prakash et al., 2008; Teraishi et al., 2004; Versteilen et al., 2011; Versteilen et al., 2006), as we have confirmed using kidney injury molecule-1 (Kim-1) as a marker (Figure 7c and d).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kentrup et al., 2011; Prakash et al., 2008; Teraishi et al., 2004; Versteilen et al., 2011; Versteilen et al., 2006, and experimental data shown in Figure 7c and d.

claim: Hydroxyfasudil may reduce kidney injury by reducing microvascular leukocyte accumulation, possibly by increasing the activity of eNOS.
source: In addition to inhibiting pericyte-mediated capillary constriction, hydroxyfasudil may also reduce kidney injury by reducing microvascular leukocyte accumulation, possibly by increasing the activity of eNOS (Versteilen et al., 2011; Yamasowa et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is speculative, supported by citations to Versteilen et al., 2011; Yamasowa et al., 2005.

claim: Rho kinase inhibition can block optogenetically induced constriction of brain capillaries by pericytes.
source: In agreement with our findings in kidney pericytes, Rho kinase inhibition can block optogenetically induced constriction of brain capillaries by pericytes (Hartmann et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hartmann et al., 2021.

claim: Ischaemia-evoked capillary constriction reflects renal pericytes generating an actomyosin-dependent contraction.
source: Taken together, these findings support the concept that ischaemia-evoked capillary constriction reflects renal pericytes generating an actomyosin-dependent contraction, rather than there being a non-specific mechanism of constriction such as pericyte swelling.
evidence: The claim is inferred from all the experimental data presented.

claim: Hydroxyfasudil is the active metabolite of fasudil.
source: Hydroxyfasudil is the active metabolite of fasudil, a drug that has been clinically approved in Japan since 1995 for the treatment of vasospasm following subarachnoid haemorrhage (Lingor et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lingor et al., 2019.

claim: Fasudil has been clinically approved in Japan since 1995 for the treatment of vasospasm following subarachnoid haemorrhage.
source: Hydroxyfasudil is the active metabolite of fasudil, a drug that has been clinically approved in Japan since 1995 for the treatment of vasospasm following subarachnoid haemorrhage (Lingor et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lingor et al., 2019.

claim: Fasudil treatment improves stroke outcome in animal models and humans.
source: Fasudil treatment improves stroke outcome in animal models (Vesterinen et al., 2013) and humans (Shibuya et al., 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Vesterinen et al., 2013 and Shibuya et al., 2005.

claim: Fasudil may be useful for reducing post-ischaemic renal no-reflow and kidney damage.
source: and our data suggest that it may also be useful for reducing post-ischaemic renal no-reflow and kidney damage.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing hydroxyfasudil (the active metabolite of fasudil) reduces no-reflow and kidney damage.

claim: Post-ischaemic erythrocyte congestion in vasa recta has previously been described.
source: Post-ischaemic erythrocyte congestion in vasa recta has previously been described (Crislip et al., 2017; Olof et al., 1991)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Crislip et al., 2017; Olof et al., 1991.

claim: Physically adhering red blood cells do not physically cause the capillary blockages observed after ischaemia.
source: however physically adhering red blood cells do not physically cause the capillary blockages observed after ischaemia as they were associated with only a small percentage of block sites (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a, b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a, b.

claim: Red blood cell trapping could be a consequence rather than a cause of the blockages.
source: Thus, red blood cell trapping could be a consequence rather than a cause of the blockages.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing red blood cells are associated with only a small percentage of blockages.

claim: Leukocyte trapping may contribute to reducing blood flow, but occurs on a longer time scale than studied.
source: Leukocyte trapping may also contribute to reducing blood flow, but occurs on a longer time scale than we have studied (Kelly et al., 1994; Rabb et al., 1995; Ysebaert et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kelly et al., 1994; Rabb et al., 1995; Ysebaert et al., 2000.

claim: A degradation of the eGCX has been reported after ischaemia.
source: Similarly, although a degradation of the eGCX has been reported after ischaemia (Snoeijs et al., 2010; Song et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Snoeijs et al., 2010; Song et al., 2018.

claim: A uniform distribution of the eGCX along the vessel wall was found, which was not modified after ischaemia.
source: we found a uniform distribution of the eGCX along the vessel wall, which was not modified after ischaemia (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e, h)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1e, h.

claim: Pericyte-mediated constrictions of the descending vasa recta and cortical peritubular capillaries contribute to no-reflow and kidney injury at early stages of reperfusion.
source: The present study demonstrates that pericyte-mediated constrictions of the descending vasa recta and cortical peritubular capillaries contribute to no-reflow and kidney injury at early stages of reperfusion
evidence: The claim is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the experimental data.

claim: Other factors, such as inflammation and leukocyte infiltration, or eGCX dysfunction, might also contribute to post-ischaemic microvascular injury at later phases of acute kidney injury.
source: however, we cannot exclude the possibility that other factors, such as inflammation and leukocyte infiltration (Gandolfo et al., 2009; Kelly et al., 1994; Rabb et al., 1995; Ysebaert et al., 2000), or eGCX dysfunction (Bongoni et al., 2019), might also contribute to post-ischaemic microvascular injury at later phases of acute kidney injury.
evidence: The claim is speculative, acknowledging limitations of the study and supported by citations.

claim: In response to the pericyte-mediated constriction evoked by ischaemia, the DVR may undergo post-ischaemic adaptations, releasing more nitric oxide at 48 hr post-ischaemia which could reduce pericyte constriction at later times after ischaemia.
source: Furthermore, in response to the pericyte-mediated constriction evoked by ischaemia, the DVR may undergo post-ischaemic adaptations, releasing more nitric oxide at 48 hr post-ischaemia which could reduce pericyte constriction at later times after ischaemia than we have studied (Zhang et al., 2018b).
evidence: The claim is speculative, supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2018b.

claim: The recovery of blood flow in the medulla on renal arterial reperfusion was slower than in the cortex.
source: The recovery of blood flow in the medulla on renal arterial reperfusion was slower than in the cortex.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a and b.

claim: The regulation of renal medullary blood flow is mainly mediated by vasa recta pericytes, independent of total or cortical blood flow.
source: The regulation of renal medullary blood flow is mainly mediated by vasa recta pericytes, independent of total or cortical blood flow (Pallone and Silldorff, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pallone and Silldorff, 2001.

claim: Pericytes on the DVR are much closer together (mean separation 22.9 ± 0.9 µm) and with more circumferential processes than peritubular cortical pericytes (mean separation 41.3 ± 2.6 µm) which have mainly longitudinal (strand-like) processes.
source: The need for accurate flow regulation in the relatively hypoxic medulla may account for pericytes on the DVR being much closer together (mean separation 22.9 ± 0.9 µm) and with more circumferential processes (Figure 4a–c, Figure 4—figure supplement 2b) than for peritubular cortical pericytes (mean separation 41.3 ± 2.6 µm) which have mainly longitudinal (strand-like) processes (Figure 5a–c, Figure 4—figure supplement 2a)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from measurements of pericyte spacing and morphology.

claim: The greater pericyte density and morphology in the DVR may contribute to a greater pericyte-mediated restriction of blood flow after ischaemia in the DVR than in the cortical capillaries.
source: and this may, in turn, contribute to a greater pericyte-mediated restriction of blood flow after ischaemia in the DVR than in the cortical capillaries.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data on pericyte density and morphology differences between medulla and cortex.

claim: Cortical and medullary pericytes showed similar immunoreactivity changes for p-MLC after ischaemia/reperfusion and hydroxyfasudil treatment.
source: Despite these morphological differences between cortical and medullary pericytes, they showed similar immunoreactivity changes for p-MLC after ischaemia/reperfusion and hydroxyfasudil treatment (Figure 6a–j).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6a–j.

claim: In post-cadaveric renal transplants, a better outcome has been reported for kidneys with a higher number of pericytes immediately post-transplant.
source: Perhaps surprisingly, given our data, in post-cadaveric renal transplants a better outcome has been reported for kidneys with a higher number of pericytes immediately post-transplant (Kwon et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kwon et al., 2008.

claim: The better outcome for kidneys with more pericytes may reflect an aspect of pericyte function other than capillary constriction, such as angiogenesis and maintenance of vessel integrity.
source: This may, however, reflect an aspect of pericyte function other than capillary constriction, such as angiogenesis and maintenance of vessel integrity (Shaw et al., 2018), with these functions failing in transplanted tissue in which pericytes have already died due to ischaemia.
evidence: The claim is speculative, supported by a citation to Shaw et al., 2018.

claim: In the brain, heart, and retina, contractile pericytes on capillaries play a key role in producing a prolonged reduction of blood flow after ischaemia.
source: In the brain, heart, and retina, contractile pericytes on capillaries play a key role in producing a prolonged reduction of blood flow after ischaemia (Hall et al., 2014; O'Farrell et al., 2017; Yemisci et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hall et al., 2014; O'Farrell et al., 2017; Yemisci et al., 2009.

claim: The kidney largely depends on the renal artery to provide a non-anastomotic supply to the glomeruli of each nephro-vascular unit.
source: In contrast, the kidney largely depends on the renal artery to provide a non-anastomotic supply to the glomeruli of each nephro-vascular unit (Evans et al., 2013; Pallone et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Evans et al., 2013; Pallone et al., 2012.

claim: Medullary hypoxia under normal conditions has been documented in several mammalian species, including humans.
source: Medullary hypoxia under normal conditions has been documented in several mammalian species, including humans (Epstein et al., 1982; Leonhardt and Landes, 1963).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Epstein et al., 1982; Leonhardt and Landes, 1963.

claim: The medullary partial pressure of oxygen is ~10–20 mm Hg, contrasting with the partial pressure of oxygen in the cortex, which is ~50 mm Hg.
source: The medullary partial pressure of oxygen is ~10–20 mm Hg, contrasting with the partial pressure of oxygen in the cortex, which is ~50 mm Hg (Brezis et al., 1994a; Brezis et al., 1991; Brezis et al., 1994b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brezis et al., 1994a; Brezis et al., 1991; Brezis et al., 1994b.

claim: Renal pericytes, especially in the medulla, are likely to be more susceptible to ischaemic injury than in other organs.
source: Thus, renal pericytes, especially in the medulla, are likely to be more susceptible to ischaemic injury than in other organs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data on medullary hypoxia.

claim: Unilateral ischaemia without contralateral nephrectomy was chosen to explore the early mechanisms of ischaemia and reperfusion injury while using the contralateral kidney as a paired control.
source: In the present study, unilateral ischaemia without contralateral nephrectomy (which may occur during renal-sparing surgeries) (Hollenbeck et al., 2006; Medina-Rico et al., 2017) was chosen to explore the early mechanisms of ischaemia and reperfusion injury while using the contralateral kidney as a paired control for potential systemic haemodynamic changes that could be triggered during and after the surgical procedure.
evidence: The claim explains the experimental design choice, supported by citations to Hollenbeck et al., 2006; Medina-Rico et al., 2017.

claim: The presence of an uninjured contralateral kidney reduces animal mortality during the surgical procedure, and thus longer ischaemia times can be used, resulting in more severe and reproducible injury.
source: The presence of an uninjured contralateral kidney reduces animal mortality during the surgical procedure, and thus longer ischaemia times can be used, resulting in more severe and reproducible injury (Fu et al., 2018; Le Clef et al., 2016; Polichnowski et al., 2020; Soranno et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fu et al., 2018; Le Clef et al., 2016; Polichnowski et al., 2020; Soranno et al., 2019.

claim: Unilateral ischaemia-reperfusion without contralateral nephrectomy is considered a strong model to study the progression from acute renal injury to long-term tubulo-interstitial fibrosis.
source: Unilateral ischaemia-reperfusion without contralateral nephrectomy is considered a strong model to study the progression from acute renal injury to long-term tubulo-interstitial fibrosis (Fu et al., 2018; Le Clef et al., 2016; Polichnowski et al., 2020; Soranno et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fu et al., 2018; Le Clef et al., 2016; Polichnowski et al., 2020; Soranno et al., 2019.

claim: All experiments were performed on male rats and mice.
source: A limitation of our study is that all experiments were performed on male rats and mice.
evidence: The claim is an explicit statement about the study design.

claim: Female rats are relatively protected against post-ischaemic renal failure.
source: Female rats are relatively protected against post-ischaemic renal failure (Lima-Posada et al., 2017; Müller et al., 2002)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lima-Posada et al., 2017; Müller et al., 2002.

claim: In male rats, androgens promote ischaemic kidney damage by triggering endothelin-induced vascular constriction.
source: possibly because in male rats androgens promote ischaemic kidney damage by triggering endothelin-induced vascular constriction (Müller et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Müller et al., 2002.

claim: Sex did not influence ischaemia reperfusion-induced injury after 24 hr, but only after 7 days.
source: However, these studies showed that sex did not influence ischaemia repefusion-induced injury after 24 hr, but only after 7 days (Lima-Posada et al., 2017; Müller et al., 2002), which is on a much longer time scale than we have studied.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lima-Posada et al., 2017; Müller et al., 2002.

claim: Pericyte contraction contributes to reducing cortical and medullary blood flow at early stages of reperfusion.
source: In the present study, we have shown that pericyte contraction contributes to reducing cortical and medullary blood flow at early stages of reperfusion.
evidence: The claim is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the experimental data.

claim: The initial pattern of pericyte contraction could contribute to the pericyte injury, detachment and capillary rarefaction observed at later stages after ischaemia and reperfusion.
source: This initial pattern could also contribute to the pericyte injury, detachment and capillary rarefaction observed at later stages after ischaemia and reperfusion (Kramann et al., 2017), which lead to further damage to the kidney (Khairoun et al., 2013; Kramann et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is speculative, supported by citations to Kramann et al., 2017; Khairoun et al., 2013.

claim: There was no evidence of pericyte detachment during the time frame of the present study.
source: However, there was no evidence of pericyte detachment during the time frame of the present study.
evidence: The claim is based on observations during the study.

claim: Treatment from the beginning of reperfusion with hydroxyfasudil increased medullary and cortical blood flow, increased the post-ischaemic diameter of DVR capillaries at pericyte locations, reduced the percentage of DVR capillaries that remained blocked, and reduced kidney injury after renal reperfusion.
source: Treatment from the beginning of reperfusion (to mimic a clinically possible therapeutic approach) with hydroxyfasudil, a Rho kinase inhibitor, increased medullary and cortical blood flow, increased the post-ischaemic diameter of DVR capillaries at pericyte locations, reduced the percentage of DVR capillaries that remained blocked, and reduced kidney injury after renal reperfusion.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main experimental findings of the study.

claim: The protection of renal blood flow and downstream tissue health would be even greater if hydroxyfasudil could be given before ischaemia was induced.
source: Presumably, the protection of renal blood flow and downstream tissue health would be even greater if hydroxyfasudil could be given before ischaemia was induced (e.g. in situations such as cardiac surgery and kidney transplantation, where renal ischaemia might be anticipated).
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferring that pre-treatment would be more effective than treatment at reperfusion.

claim: Pericytes are a novel therapeutic target for reducing no-reflow after renal ischaemia.
source: Thus, pericytes are a novel therapeutic target for reducing no-reflow after renal ischaemia.
evidence: The claim is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Acute kidney injury caused by post-ischaemic no-reflow causes significant socio-economic cost.
source: Acute kidney injury caused by post-ischaemic no-reflow causes significant socio-economic cost.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge about the impact of acute kidney injury.

claim: The identification of pericyte contraction as a therapeutic target for ischaemia-induced acute kidney injury should contribute to the development or re-purposing of drugs that can prevent renal no-reflow.
source: Our identification ofpericyte contraction as a therapeutic target for ischaemia-induced acute kidney injury should contribute to the development or re-purposing of drugs that can prevent renal no-reflow.
evidence: The claim is the main implication of the study's findings.
